newsitem.title: UK: German gold reserves plan deflates market.
newsitem.headline: German gold reserves plan deflates market.

text.p: The possibility that Germany may revalue its gold reserves pushed the price of the metal lower in Europe on Thursday morning.

Germany's Ministry of Finance confirmed that Finance Minister Theo Waigel would be discussing a proposal to revalue the country's 2,956 tonnes of gold reserves at the Bundesbank Council meeting later today.
Initial reaction from many gold market participants mirrored the opinion of a Frankfurt based dealer who said "It is not good news for the gold market."

Reports of the proposal appeared on Wednesday evening and knocked about $2.00 per ounce off the gold price in New York. This morning gold was fixed in London at $347.10 per ounce, down a dollar from the Wednesday afternoon fixing.
"The dollar was weaker against the yen overnight which encouraged some buying in the Far East," a dealer said, adding "it had done well" to resist pressure to take it even lower.

Revaluing Germany's gold reserves closer to the market price than their 144-mark ($85.05) an ounce book value, would allow the government to release billions of "hidden" reserves to offset deficits and arguably avoid raising taxes.

Germany, once the star candidate for EMU membership, is seeking desperately to rein in its budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product or less to make sure it qualifies for the euro's launch in 1999.
The issue has become yet more urgent as experts from federal, state and local governments are expected to announce a shortfall of 20 billion marks ($12 billion) in tax revenues later on Thursday.
"The German stories are not new. Junior partners in the government there have been advocating selling gold to avoid raising taxes for a long time," a gold dealer said.

As well as considering its gold reserves, the German government announcemed on Wednesday that Bonn is considering an early sale of some of its Deutsche Telekom shares as another means of raising revenue.
"But at the moment they cannot do either of these things. There have to be changes in the laws" the Frankfurt-based gold trader said.
The Bundesbank selling gold to reduce the country's government deficit as some of the minor parties in the governing coalition advocate has been ruled out by market experts.

"I can't see Germany selling gold after the tremendous amount of noise they have made about the IMF (International Monetary Fund) proposing to sell from its reserves," said metals markets analyst Rhona O'Connell at stockbroker T. Hoare and Co.
She said successive German governments' deep seated fear of inflation meant they preferred to have some solid assets in their reserves.
"I can see them selling DeutscheTelekom but not gold," O'Connell added.
Even so, the impact on the gold market of a change of philosophy by the staunchest advocate of the metal as a reserve could be significant.
"Forget the small print, it's being talked about," said one senior dealer, adding that the market was right not to worry about details and sell gold on the initial news.
"For whatever reason Germany is getting real. Like in Switzerland (which proposed revaluing its gold reserves earlier this year) the move has come from domestic pressure," the senior dealer added.

The gold price has been depressed for months under the cloud of threatened sales by the European central banks as they jockey their economies into meeting the Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria for Eurppeam Monetary Union by the end of next year.
But only the Netherlands has admitted selling gold when in January it revealed it had sold 300 tonnes of metal late last year.
The market seemed to have steadied recently after slipping to its lowest price in four years of $336.90 in February. But that is less certain now, dealers and analysts said.
"Just when it seemed safe to go back in, up pops another central bank," said O'Connell.
